A raffle is a competition in which people buy numbered tickets for a chance to win a prize. No skill or knowledge is involved — the winner is chosen purely by luck. At the end of the raffle, someone draws a ticket number at random from all the tickets that were sold, and whoever holds the matching ticket wins the prize.

Here is how it works in practice. Each raffle ticket has a unique number. When you buy one, you keep one half of it (called the stub) and the other half goes into a container — a box, a bag, or a spinning drum. Once all the tickets have been sold (or the set deadline has passed), someone reaches in without looking and pulls out one stub. The number on that stub is announced, and the person holding the matching half wins. Some raffles have multiple prizes, so multiple stubs are drawn.

The prize in a raffle can be almost anything — a sum of money, a car, a holiday, a television, a food hamper, or even a small gift. The bigger and more desirable the prize, the more people want to buy tickets.

Raffles are very commonly used to raise money for a cause — a school, a charity, a sports club, or a local community organisation. People pay for their tickets, that money goes to the cause, and one lucky ticket-holder wins the prize. This makes a raffle one of the most popular fundraising methods, because people are happy to pay for the excitement of possibly winning something. That said, raffles are not always charitable — they are also held at fairs, festivals, and parties simply for fun.

The single most important thing to understand about a raffle is that luck is the only deciding factor. It does not matter who you are, how much you know, or how experienced you are. Buying more tickets does improve your statistical chances (because more of your numbers are in the draw), but even a single ticket gives you a genuine shot at winning. This is what makes raffles feel exciting and fair to everyone — absolutely anyone can win.

It is also worth knowing how a raffle differs from similar things. A lottery is essentially the same concept, but on a much larger scale — usually run by governments, with millions of participants and very large cash prizes. A raffle is typically smaller, more local, and more community-based. An auction is different because the highest bidder wins, not a random draw. A competition or contest is different because it rewards skill; in a raffle, skill plays no part whatsoever.

As a noun, the word refers to the event or competition itself. For example: "The school is holding a raffle to raise money for new computers." "She won a weekend trip in the raffle." "He bought ten tickets for the raffle hoping to win the car."
